blocks.text: Hypoglycaemia is a clinical and biochemical condition characterised by an abnormally low blood glucose concentration, which may result in autonomic activation, neuroglycopenia, impaired consciousness, seizures, coma and, if prolonged, permanent neurological injury or death.
In adults with diabetes, the American Diabetes Association (ADA) uses a glucose concentration of less than 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) as an alert threshold requiring action.
The ADA classifies hypoglycaemia into three levels.

rows: Severe event requiring assistance because of altered physical or mental functioning

blocks.text: **Clinical note:** These are diabetes-management thresholds, not universal diagnostic criteria for every person without diabetes. In people without diabetes, investigation generally focuses on Whipple's triad:

items.text: Symptoms or signs consistent with hypoglycaemia.

rows: Confusion, behavioural changes, difficulty concentrating, visual disturbance
Seizures, unconsciousness, coma, inability to self-treat

blocks.text: Hypoglycaemia can occur in patients with diabetes receiving glucose-lowering medication and in individuals without diabetes.
This is the most common cause in people with diabetes.

blocks.text: Other contributors include medication errors, accidental insulin administration, wrong insulin concentration and failure to adjust doses during fasting or illness.

blocks.text: **Clinical pearl:** A patient with severe malaria who develops altered consciousness should have blood glucose checked immediately. Hypoglycaemia may coexist with cerebral malaria and can independently cause neurological deterioration.

blocks.title: The objectives of treatment are to:

items.text: Restore blood glucose to a safe concentration.
Prevent seizures, coma and neurological injury.
Identify and treat the underlying cause.
Review and correct the causative medication or precipitating factor.
Educate patients and caregivers on prevention.

blocks.text: Hypoglycaemia is a time-critical emergency. Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for laboratory confirmation when a reliable bedside glucose reading is low and the patient is symptomatic.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Discharge prescriptions, follow-up and high-yield clinical pearls

blocks.title: A patient treated for hypoglycaemia may be considered for discharge when:

items.text: Blood glucose has returned to a safe range.
The patient can eat and drink normally.
There is no evidence of ongoing insulin or sulfonylurea effect requiring hospital monitoring.
The precipitating cause has been identified or appropriately investigated.
The patient understands how to prevent and treat another episode.

blocks.text: **Do not discharge prematurely** after severe, recurrent, unexplained or sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia.

For a patient with type 2 diabetes who experienced hypoglycaemia from a sulfonylurea, the causative medication should be reviewed and potentially discontinued. The replacement diabetes regimen depends on renal function, HbA1c, comorbidities and individual glycaemic targets.
